{"id": "4:1/q60", "question": "What status do the seven readings and performance variants have?", "turns_on": "How sound chains, codex agreement, Arabic grammar, and performance transmission are weighed.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q60/p1", "position": "A sound reading depends on transmission and valid Arabic rather than grammatical preference alone", "reasons": "Al-Burhān distinguishes Qurʾān and its readings, gives reading manuals, reports majority mutawātir status and Abū Shāma's chain qualification, and defends transmitted pronunciation variants including hamza, lengthening, and imāla."}, {"id": "4:1/q60/p2", "position": "Variants of a given reading may be famous without every chain being mass transmitted", "reasons": "Abū Shāma notes single-transmitter stretches; Ibn al-Ḥājib questions performance features, while al-Burhān says shared categories are transmitted even if their measured degree varies."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q61", "question": "How do rhetorical order and omission help explain this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q61/p1", "position": "Order, specified terms, and contextual ellipsis guide emphasis and sense", "reasons": "Al-Burhān treats the single soul as an allusion to Adam, discusses a specified member after a general class, permissible conjunct attachment, deletion with sufficient contextual indication, and ordering by rank or cause; it includes related examples elsewhere in the Qurʾān."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q62", "question": "How should the two fear commands relate to each other?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q62/p1", "position": "Both address the original audience, with the second confirming and specifying the first", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī objects to making the second alone Arab-specific; the first stresses shared creation and the second God-invoked social obligations."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q63", "question": "What is the inward reading of God's name and kinship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q63/p1", "position": "Asking by God denies independent existence; true kinship binds saints and higher principles", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says loving saints preserves spiritual ties and prevents estrangement from the Real."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q64", "question": "What grammatical analogies bear on coordination and agreement here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q64/p1", "position": "Coordination to pronouns, deletion of conjunctions, and agreement by noun or sense have competing analyses", "reasons": "Al-Burhān compares nominative and genitive pronoun conjunctions, Ibn Mālik's clause analysis, al-Fārisī's repeated-preposition rule, and a disagreement over feminine agreement in a separate nafs verse; another ordering ranks unseen above seen."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q65", "question": "How does al-Bursawī explain common origin and kinship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q65/p1", "position": "Common descent and faith create duties of mutual care, while the spouse and family bond support reproduction", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says women, family, and ancestral descent call people to preserve rights; he distinguishes people of the revelation and later generations from earlier people, and adds a spiritual warning against neglecting divine watchfulness."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q66", "question": "What do the two gender nouns denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q66/p1", "position": "They mark the male and female human kinds", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī distinguishes rijāl from women and cites 33:40."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q68", "question": "How does Elmalılı reason from present reproduction to the first pair?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q68/p1", "position": "Successive generations can be traced back to one first pair; Eve's miraculous branching and the complementary pair display divine creation", "reasons": "Elmalılı calls fathers prior in fertilization but says neither can reproduce alone. {"id": "4:1/q69", "question": "What readings and interpretations of the kinship appeal does Elmalılı distinguish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q69/p1", "position": "Ḥamza's genitive favors an appeal by God and kinship, while the accusative also supports a direct duty not to neglect kin", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the appeal interpretation works under both cases, while the explicit legal command requires the non-genitive analysis; the first brings law forward, the second moral mercy."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q70", "question": "How does Elmalılı connect gender, rights, and the divine command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q70/p1", "position": "Universal brotherhood and family bonds require protection of women's dignity, responsible sexuality, and compassion governed by taqwā", "reasons": "Elmalılı distinguishes the opening universal warning from the later family warning; he says selfish desire must not defeat divine commands and reports the Prophet's praise of a righteous spouse."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q71", "question": "What broader duties does Elmalılı derive from human creation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q71/p1", "position": "Creation from a single pair calls for brotherhood, marriage, procreation, nurturing offspring, and obedience to a Creator beyond nature", "reasons": "Elmalılı rejects autonomous nature as the explanation of diverse offspring, cites Iblīs's erroneous nature argument, and reports the Prophet's encouragement of marriage and procreation."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q72", "question": "What additional glosses does Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmit?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q72/p1", "position": "Created can mean made; a report interprets woman's derivation from man as an explanation of attraction", "reasons": "Al-Suddī supplies the lexical gloss, while Ibn ʿAbbās's report says woman desires men and man desires earth, then counsels restraint."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q73", "question": "What does Ibn ʿĀshūr see in the opening's creation language?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q73/p1", "position": "The wondrous creation supports a universal summons, reciprocal benefit between spouses, and laws founded on lineage", "reasons": "He says the Prophet has a special kinship claim on polytheists; the spouse recalls al-Baqara, and both sexes benefit through mutual pairing and offspring."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q74", "question": "How does Ibn ʿĀshūr read the family-rights command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q74/p1", "position": "The accusative commands regard for relatives' rights, while the genitive recalls Arabs' reverent appeal by kinship and reproves neglect of those very relatives", "reasons": "He cites ʿUtba's appeal, criticizes al-Mubarrad's categorical grammatical rejection, and connects the wording with harm to orphan kin and even to Muhammad despite his blood relation."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q75", "question": "What broader praise of Qurʾān study is transmitted near this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q75/p1", "position": "Learning, teaching, reciting, and following the Qurʾān are praised in reports collected by Ibn ʿAṭiyya", "reasons": "The reports include the Prophet's saying about learning and teaching, Ibn Masʿūd's preference for recitation, Jesus' praise of following scripture, signs of late moral reversal, and extraordinary recitation accounts."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q76", "question": "What additional language evidence does Ibn ʿAṭiyya cite?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q76/p1", "position": "Bathth is dispersal; Basran grammarians object to genitive coordination; raqīb is close, verifying observation", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites 101:4 for bathth, Sībawayh's poetic-license rule and Abū ʿAlī's weak-analogy view, and a watcher in the arrow game with Abū Duʾād's poem."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q97", "question": "What other analyses of al-arḥām does al-Samīn record?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q97/p1", "position": "The accusative singles out kinship under general fear of God; the genitive can be an oath or omit a prior preposition", "reasons": "Al-Samīn notes Abū al-Baqāʾ's implied 'Lord of kinship' and exaltation reading, al-Farrāʾ's uneasy acceptance, and that God can swear by creatures though the verse's sense is not an oath."}]}

{"id": "4:23/q07", "question": "Which sisters are forbidden?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q07/p1", "position": "Full, paternal half, and maternal half-sisters are included.", "reasons": "The listed commentators take the shared parent in either line to establish sisterhood."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q08", "question": "Which aunts are forbidden?", "turns_on": "How auntship follows male or female ancestors, including cross-line cases.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q08/p1", "position": "Sisters of male ancestors are paternal aunts; sisters of female ancestors are maternal aunts, however remote.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Ṭabrisī expressly include maternal grandfathers' sisters and paternal grandmothers' sisters; al-Ālūsī distinguishes an aunt of an aunt by the connecting blood line."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q09", "question": "Which nieces are forbidden?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q09/p1", "position": "Daughters and further female descendants of every brother or sister, including half-siblings, are forbidden.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī compares their scope to daughters; Abū Ḥayyān explains the singular sibling nouns as generic."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q10", "question": "What does nursing establish between the child and a family?", "turns_on": "Whether the milk-producing husband is included, and how far the lineage analogy extends.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q10/p1", "position": "Nursing reproduces the seven lineage prohibitions through nurse and milk father.", "reasons": "The Prophetic rule is repeatedly transmitted; al-Rāzī sees mothers and sisters as birth and sibling examples that imply the rest. Commentators trace grandparents, aunts, and siblings through the nurse and husband."}, {"id": "4:23/q10/p2", "position": "The milk father does not generate kinship prohibition.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, al-Nakhaʿī, and Abū Salama deny transmission through the husband. Al-Qurṭubī says milk comes from the woman, while the father only caused conception."}, {"id": "4:23/q10/p3", "position": "The milk father does generate corresponding paternal kinship.", "reasons": "The majority attribute milk to the husband whose child caused it; the four Sunni schools and several commentators apply the lineage hadith."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q11", "question": "What exceptions are claimed to the nursing-lineage analogy?", "turns_on": "Whether apparent exceptions concern affinity rather than lineage.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q11/p1", "position": "A man may marry his milk son's sister or his milk brother's mother.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū Ḥayyān say the blood prohibitions in these cases come from sexual affinity absent in nursing; al-Bayḍāwī makes the same distinction."}, {"id": "4:23/q11/p2", "position": "The analogy has no true lineage exceptions.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr rejects lists of four or six purported exceptions because their examples involve affinity or already exist in blood kinship; investigators cited by al-Ālūsī agree."}, {"id": "4:23/q11/p3", "position": "Numerous exceptions exist.", "reasons": "Al-Baḥr is reported by al-Ālūsī to count eighty-one; the note does not list them."}]}

{"id": "4:23/q13", "question": "At what age does nursing still create a marriage bar?", "turns_on": "Whether nourishment before weaning, a fixed two years, later months, or adult nursing controls.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q13/p1", "position": "The limit is two full years or infancy before effective weaning.", "reasons": "The majority cite 2:233 and reports that nursing is from hunger; Ibn ʿĀshūr makes nutritive dependence central and treats the Salim case as special."}, {"id": "4:23/q13/p2", "position": "Abū Ḥanīfa allows thirty months.", "reasons": "Reports in al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr give two and a half years."}, {"id": "4:23/q13/p3", "position": "Mālik is reported to allow some period beyond two years.", "reasons": "Versions range from days or one month to two or three months or continued need for milk; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports distinct transmissions."}, {"id": "4:23/q13/p4", "position": "Adult nursing can establish the relation.", "reasons": "Aisha, al-Layth, and Dāwūd cite the adult Salim dispensation; other wives and the majority treat it as specific, while Abū Mūsā reportedly retracted."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q14", "question": "What manner of milk delivery counts as nursing?", "turns_on": "Whether milk must pass from the breast by the mouth, or other delivery reaching the stomach suffices.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q14/p1", "position": "Milk reaching the infant's stomach by mouth or nose counts even without sucking.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī and al-Khāniya define the operative cause as human milk reaching the stomach and exclude ear, wound, or enema delivery and uncertain intake."}, {"id": "4:23/q14/p2", "position": "Only ordinary breast-to-mouth feeding counts.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports his school's exclusion of poured, nasal, enema, and dead-woman's milk."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q15", "question": "When does a wife's mother become forbidden?", "turns_on": "Whether the later consummation condition reaches mothers-in-law as well as stepdaughters.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q15/p1", "position": "A valid marriage contract with her daughter forbids her, regardless of consummation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, and most commentators cite the unqualified clause, syntax, consensus, and the Prophetic distinction between mother and stepdaughter; Ibn Masʿūd reportedly withdrew his contrary view."}, {"id": "4:23/q15/p2", "position": "Consummation with the daughter is required.", "reasons": "Reports attribute this to ʿAlī, Zayd, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn al-Zubayr, Jābir, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Mujāhid; they apply the one later condition to both clauses. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers it on parallel rationale."}, {"id": "4:23/q15/p3", "position": "Zayd distinguishes divorce before consummation from death.", "reasons": "In reports through al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, and others, divorce permits the mother but death with inheritance bars her; al-Rāzī analogizes death to consummation for waiting-period rules."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q16", "question": "How does tanwin behave in compound vocatives?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q16/p1", "position": "It remains inside an incomplete vocative phrase, but may drop at a completed name's end.", "reasons": "Sībawayh compares compound numerals with participial and comparative vocatives, and distinguishes annexation to an indefinite noun."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q17", "question": "How do verbal nouns govern their arguments?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q17/p1", "position": "Verbal nouns can govern objects, agents, and adverbials with verbal force, while tanwin and annexation affect case.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites 90:14-15, Ruʾbah, al-Murār al-Asadī, and other verse and poetry. He rejects one adjectival analogy that al-Khalīl accepts."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q18", "question": "How can an accusative verbal noun emphasize an assertion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q18/p1", "position": "An understood verb governs an accusative verbal noun used to reinforce an earlier statement or oath.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives ʿurfan, qasaman, Qur'anic examples such as ṣunʿ Allāh and waʿd Allāh, and a shepherd's poem; a nominative can instead supply an implied subject."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q19", "question": "Does a variant reading qualify mothers-in-law?", "turns_on": "Reliability and legal force of the reported added consummation phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q19/p1", "position": "A reported reading adds the consummation condition after mothers-in-law.", "reasons": "Attributed to ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Zayd, Ibn ʿUmar, and Ibn al-Zubayr; Ibn ʿAbbās reportedly swore this was revealed. Other transmissions deny his reading, and Shaykh al-Islām calls it weak or abrogated."}, {"id": "4:23/q19/p2", "position": "The received reading leaves mothers-in-law unqualified.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ reportedly denied Ibn ʿAbbās's added reading; al-Ṭabarī and others rely on the unqualified wording."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q20", "question": "Who is a rabība and why is she called that?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q20/p1", "position": "A wife's daughter by another man, named for a stepfather's usual upbringing of her.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī derives rabība from marbūba; al-Zajjāj and al-Ṭabrisī explain the passive sense, even when she did not actually live with or get raised by him."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q21", "question": "Does being 'in your care' legally condition the stepdaughter prohibition?", "turns_on": "Whether customary household language limits the ban after consummation.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q21/p1", "position": "No; it describes the usual household situation or its rationale.", "reasons": "Most scholars cite the explicit no-intercourse exception, not a no-residence exception. {"id": "4:23/q22", "question": "What does 'in your ḥujūr' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether it denotes physical homes or figurative care.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q22/p1", "position": "Under one's care, protection, upbringing, or in one's lap.", "reasons": "Lexicographers trace ḥijr to the lap or front fold of a garment; metaphorically it denotes guardianship. Al-Kumayt's line is cited for places of upbringing."}, {"id": "4:23/q22/p2", "position": "In one's houses.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda gives the direct household gloss; Ibn Kathīr repeats it."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q23", "question": "What is meant by entering upon a wife?", "turns_on": "Whether entry denotes intercourse, seclusion, or intimate preliminaries.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q23/p1", "position": "It euphemizes intercourse.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāwūs, al-Ṭabarī, and others take sexual intercourse as decisive; ordinary seclusion alone is insufficient for the stepdaughter bar."}, {"id": "4:23/q23/p2", "position": "Exposure, seclusion, or other sexual access can count as entry.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ includes bringing in, uncovering, and sitting between a woman's legs even at her family home; al-Bayḍāwī describes entry behind a curtain. Jurists extend the effect to lustful contact."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q24", "question": "Can touching or looking create the affinity prohibition without intercourse?", "turns_on": "Which acts count as sexual access and whether desire is required.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q24/p1", "position": "Lustful touching, kissing, or undressing can create it.", "reasons": "The majority named by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī include sexual enjoyment. Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Thawrī and others extend the effect to the mother, daughter, father, and son; al-Ālūsī cites a mursal report."}, {"id": "4:23/q24/p2", "position": "Only intercourse itself creates the stepdaughter prohibition.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāwūs, and ʿAmr ibn Dīnār distinguish intercourse from mere preliminaries; al-Ṭabarī favors this reading."}, {"id": "4:23/q24/p3", "position": "A pleasurable gaze alone can suffice.", "reasons": "Mālik includes looking at hair or beauty; Kufans require a lustful view of the genitals; al-Thawrī requires deliberateness, while al-Qurṭubī argues gaze is enjoyment."}, {"id": "4:23/q24/p4", "position": "Looking alone does not suffice.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Laylā and al-Shāfiʿī require touching; the precise lines of disagreement vary by school and report."}]}

r intercourse itself is the operative cause.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q25/p1", "position": "No; zina has none of marriage's affinity effects.", "reasons": "Mālik's sound view, al-Shāfiʿī, and al-Qurṭubī reason that an adulteress is neither a wife nor her daughter a stepdaughter; a Prophetic report says unlawful sex does not forbid lawful marriage."}, {"id": "4:23/q25/p2", "position": "Yes; illicit intercourse can cause the same affinity bar.", "reasons": "Iraqi jurists and reports from several early authorities treat intercourse as the cause because it can produce offspring; al-Ālūsī argues lawful status is irrelevant and cites forbidden intercourse parallels."}, {"id": "4:23/q25/p3", "position": "Sodomy does not create affinity.", "reasons": "Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Abū Ḥanīfa and their followers deny the effect."}, {"id": "4:23/q25/p4", "position": "Sodomy or sexual play with a boy may create affinity.", "reasons": "Al-Thawrī and Aḥmad report restrictions involving the boy's mother, a wife's male kin, or the boy's later daughter."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q26", "question": "When may a man marry the daughter of an unconsummated former wife?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q26/p1", "position": "After divorce or death ending the marriage, she is lawful.", "reasons": "The no-blame clause explicitly supplies the permission; al-Ṭabarī and many others distinguish it from the unconditional mother-in-law bar. {"id": "4:23/q27", "question": "What does ḥalāʾil mean and where does the name come from?", "turns_on": "Whether the derivation is lawfulness, cohabitation, or loosening a garment.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q27/p1", "position": "It means sons' wives; ḥalīla is derived from being lawful to a spouse.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj analyzes a woman made lawful; al-Samīn objects that the feminine ending is unusual for a passive form unless lexicalized."}, {"id": "4:23/q27/p2", "position": "It means sons' wives; the name comes from living or lodging together.", "reasons": "Al-Layth, Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Qurtubi derive it from shared dwelling or bed; poetry uses the word for a female neighbor and for a husband."}, {"id": "4:23/q27/p3", "position": "It means sons' wives; the name evokes spouses loosening one another's garments.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and others connect the term with ḥall, untying; sources record this as an alternative etymology."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q28", "question": "Which sons are meant by 'from your loins'?", "turns_on": "Whether foster sons and descendants fall within the rule despite the biological qualifier.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q28/p1", "position": "Biological sons and their descendants are included; adopted sons are excluded.", "reasons": "The wording removes adoption's former sonship, while grandsons through sons or daughters remain born descendants. {"id": "4:23/q29", "question": "When does a son's wife become forbidden to his father?", "turns_on": "Whether contract alone or consummation is required, and whether ḥalīla extends to a slave woman.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q29/p1", "position": "The valid marriage contract alone makes her forbidden.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, and others report agreement; divorce before consummation does not lift the father's bar."}, {"id": "4:23/q29/p2", "position": "The son's owned slave woman is also his ḥalīla and is barred to his father.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī and al-Rāzī argue the word covers one lawful by ownership or cohabitation; al-Biqāʿī includes concubines."}, {"id": "4:23/q29/p3", "position": "The word directly denotes a wife; other intercourse prohibitions use separate evidence.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī distinguish the textual wife from owned or illicitly approached women; mere purchase does not prohibit her to the buyer's father or son."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q30", "question": "What event is reported behind the biological-son wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q30/p1", "position": "The Prophet married Zayd ibn Ḥāritha's former wife, prompting objection because Zayd had been adopted.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ and later sources link 4:23 with 33:4, 33:37, or 33:40, which deny adoption as biological descent."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q31", "question": "How is the clause 'and that you combine two sisters' construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q31/p1", "position": "The infinitive clause is nominative and coordinated with the prohibited list.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās, al-Wāḥidī, and many later grammarians paraphrase it as the act of combining sisters being forbidden."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q32", "question": "May two sisters be married at the same time?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q32/p1", "position": "No, though either may be married after the other bond ends.", "reasons": "The verse bars the combination, including sisters by nursing; reports on converts with two sister-wives direct them to choose one. Ibn Kathīr cites consensus."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q33", "question": "May a man have intercourse with two owned sisters?", "turns_on": "Whether the marriage prohibition restricts the owned-women permission of 4:24.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q33/p1", "position": "No; joint ownership is possible but sexual combination is forbidden.", "reasons": "Most jurists apply the verse's general ban or its rationale to ownership; after intercourse with one, the other is barred until the first is effectively relinquished. Al-Rāzī prefers caution and prohibition."}, {"id": "4:23/q33/p2", "position": "Ownership permits intercourse with both sisters.", "reasons": "A literalist outlier and reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUthmān appeal to the permission for owned women; other authorities oppose this reading."}, {"id": "4:23/q33/p3", "position": "One verse permits and another forbids; the speaker refrains or suspends judgment.", "reasons": "ʿUthmān, and in some reports ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās, voice the tension but decline the practice; source accounts differ on whether this entails permission."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q34", "question": "How must an owner make the first sister unavailable before approaching the second?", "turns_on": "Whether intention or transfer, and what happens if ownership returns.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q34/p1", "position": "Dispose of ownership or create a firm bar before switching.", "reasons": "Sale, emancipation, gift, manumission contract, or marriage are cited. {"id": "4:23/q35", "question": "May a man marry his former wife's sister during her waiting period?", "turns_on": "Whether irrevocable divorce ends the combining bar immediately.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q35/p1", "position": "After irrevocable divorce, he may marry her sister immediately.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, al-Shāfiʿī and others allow it; al-Qurṭubī says this is the adopted position."}, {"id": "4:23/q35/p2", "position": "He must wait even after irrevocable divorce.", "reasons": "ʿAlī, Zayd, Mujāhid, al-Thawrī, Aḥmad, and legal rationalists require her waiting period to end; all agree in a revocable divorce."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q36", "question": "What does 'except what has passed' cover?", "turns_on": "Whether it pardons earlier acts, preserves pre-Islamic contracts, or points to earlier law.", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q36/p1", "position": "Earlier forbidden combinations are pardoned but may not continue.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, and most commentators treat the exception as disconnected. {"id": "4:23/q38", "question": "Why is the list ordered as it is?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q38/p1", "position": "The sequence moves from closest blood kin to nursing and then affinity.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī begins with mothers for their unique inviolability, sets milk sisters after milk mothers, and locates eloquence in arrangement and legal wisdom; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī describe the transition."}]}
{"id": "4:23/q39", "question": "What recitation variants are reported in this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:23/q39/p1", "position": "Variants affect ummahāt, the relative pronoun, riḍāʿa, and individual consonants.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī prefers al-Kisāʾī's fatḥa in immahāt over Ḥamza's kasra; reports also give lāʾī for lātī, Abū Ḥaywa's kasra of riḍāʿa, and softened hamza in banāt al-ukht."}, {"id": "4:23/q39/p2", "position": "Warsh's Egyptian transmissions thicken the lām in 'from your loins'.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī notes the contextual rule after ṣād, ṭāʾ, or ẓāʾ and cites this verse among ṣād-silent cases."}]}

{"id": "4:28/q01", "question": "What does God intend to lighten for people?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate marriage concession exhausts the wording or exemplifies a general principle; other readings identify repentance, temporary marriage, inward relief, or guidance as the intended relief.", "positions": [{"id": "4:28/q01/p1", "position": "He eases religious duties and burdens generally, with marriage to enslaved women among the concessions.", "reasons": "Mujahid includes every concession (MUJAHID, TAB-FULL, IBNABIHATIM). Ibn Abbas and others compare this community with the Children of Israel (WAHIDI-BASIT, RAZI-FULL); Razi cites 7:157, 2:185, 22:78.
